msDesc.head: Henricus Hassia de Langenstein, Commentaria in Genesim I–II; Germany, s. xv2/4 (before 1437)

msContents.summary: ¶ This volume is striking for its medieval limp binding, a type of binding apparently very common in the middle ages but now very rare. This one is made of an old papal bull. The volume was owned by Merton College before Lincoln and was part of the stock kept for loan to the Merton fellows: its humble appearance is revealing about the status of these electio books. The text found within is the only copy in England of a work whose circulation was limited to the German-speaking lands and which survives otherwise in German and central European libraries. The manuscript was owned by Henry of Abingdon, representative of the University of Oxford at the Council of Constance in 1415, present also at the Council of Basel in 1433; the latter was the probable venue for his acquisition of this volume.

msItem.note: Fol. 1 (so foliated) is the upper leaf of the limp cover. It is an original bull of the antipope John XXIII, dated at Constance, 18 February 1415 (12 Kal. Martii anno quinto). It is an executory mandate addressed to the bishop of Oloron, the abbot of Muchelney, and the prior of Taunton, granting an indult to Henry Abendon STP, vicar of Weston Zoyland in the diocese of Bath and Wells, to receive the fruits of this and other benefices though absent for purposes of study. (The bull is not found in the Calendar of Papal Registers, but is calendared by Major, ‘Original papal documents’, 248.) The document, which wraps around the text-block, is sewn on upside down with the writing to the inside. On the plica is written ‘Io. de Criuellis’, presumably the name of the papal notary responsible. The outer covers, originally the blank dorse, bear later notes, including a mid-fifteenth-century title, repeated underneath in the later sixteenth century: ‘Expositio super prologum sancte scripture cum variis sermonibus’; there are also names and other clues to provenance here. (See further Binding and Labels and marks and History.)

msItem.author: Henricus de Langenstein (Henricus de Hassia) (c. 1325–1397)
msItem.title: Commentary on Genesis
msItem.note: Unpr.; Stegmüller Bibl. 3188, listing sixty-five copies, including ours and an autograph of Bks XV–XIX dated 1391, which is Vienna, ÖNB, Cod. 4652. An edition is forthcoming by J. Kostoff-Kaard. The work originated as lectures delivered between 1385 and 1392 at the university of Vienna, where Henricus was vice-chancellor. Our copy begins in Bk I c. 4, meaning that the first two leaves have been lost, and lost early, for the medieval foliation does not count them. The first quire ends in II 4, ‘exempla multiformia exercende uirtutis’; the following singleton is now attached to the second quire but is the half-sheet of the lost second leaf of the first quire, for the text is continuous here, beginning ‘arguenda efficacia’ and ending on the verso, ‘intelligi possunt astrologi’. A lacuna follows: the following leaf, the first natural one of the new quire, begins, still in c. 4, ‘scripsit decades voluminum de hystoriis Romanorum’; the loss of text corresponds to one leaf and represents a lost bifolium, conjoint with fol. 1.

msItem.author: Henricus Hassia de Langenstein
msItem.title: Sermones
msItem.note: Unpr. and unnoticed by the repertories; but there is no reason to doubt the authenticity of the authorial ascriptions here, given the book’s date and provenance. There is physical loss at both ends of the booklet, with consequent losses to the text of the first and last sermons. (1) A Marian sermon; T. Hohmann, ‘Initienregister der Werke Heinrichs von Langenstein’, Traditio 32 (1976) 399–426, no. 95. (2) A rewriting by Henricus of tract. 120 from Augustine’s Tractatus in euangelium Iohannis (CPL 278); ibid. no. 234. (3) Sermo contra detractores beati Bernardi; ibid. no. 96. (4) Sermo de assumptione beatae Mariae uirginis; ibid. no. 170. (5) Sermo de conceptione beatae Mariae uirginis. This work is ascribed to the theologian Henricus de Oyta (c. 1330–1397) in Admont, Benediktinerstift, MS 163 (s. xv) and Erfurt, Universitätsbibliothek, MS CA 4o 150 (s. xv). He was associated with Henricus de Langenstein towards the end of his career, while teaching at Vienna: the two men together drew up statutes for the university in 1389. What would speak for his authorship of this sermon would be the presence of one of the manuscripts at Erfurt, a city in which Henricus held the rectorship of a school between 1355 and 1366, the year in which he returned to Prague; he taught thereafter in Paris, then Vienna. (6) Sermo de annuntiatione beatae Mariae uirginis; ibid. no. 50. (7) Sermo de natiuitate beatae Mariae uirginis; ibid. no. 112. The text breaks off with the loss of the back leaf.

Fol. 202 is the other half of the wrapper made from the papal bull described above. The writing is on the recto, upside down. In the outer margin, a table of contents for the volume has been added in an English hand in black ink, perhaps that of Henry of Abingdon and therefore written before his death in 1437 (which would be an appropriate dating for the script): ‘exposicio super prologum biblie | compotus ecclesiastica abbreuiatus | exposicio super loquente ihesu ad turbas | sermo de lancea et clauis dominicis | sermo commendatius beati barnardi | sermo de assumpcione beate marie | sermo de conceptione beate marie | sermo de annunciatione beate marie | sermo de natiuitate beate marie’.

supportDesc.support: Paper. Paper is firm and clean, a little cockled. There has been some loss to the outer leaves at the edges (2–22, 196–201), perhaps from damp, rebacked with modern paper. Losses to fol. 2 have taken away some of the text. Spinefolds have been strengthened with parchment strips. Watermarked with two common forms of the Oxhead, one resembling Piccard II (Ochsenkopf), VIII, nos. 32, 52 (attested for 1413 × 1421 with German provenances), the other IX, no. 31 (attested Basel, Neuenburg, 1419, 1411). Chainlines are horizontal.
supportDesc.extent:
i + 202 + i (limp wrapper counted as flyleaves).
298 215
200–205 115–27
supportDesc.foliation: Medieval ink foliation in arabic at the head at the outer edge of the written space. It is partial and inaccurate: first visible at 4, continuous from 6 to 42, one skipped, 43–53, one skipped, 54–65, 67 (bis), 68–71, 73 (bis), 74–75. The early twentieth-century Bodleian pencil foliation, which is followed here, was deferential to this earlier one and absorbed it, accepting the missed leaf after 42 and foliating 42a and 42b, and after 53, foliating 53a and 53b, but crossing out the first ‘67’ and foliating 66. The Bodleian count includes the limp wrapper, foliating as 1 and 202.
supportDesc.collation: 18 (fols. 2–9, lacks first, second and twelfth; eleventh is a half-sheet attached to the next quire) 212 (fols. 10–22, an added singleton from Q1 before first) 312 (fols. 23–34) 412 (fols. 35–45, ninth skipped, foliated 42b) 512 (fols. 46–56, ninth skipped, foliated 53b) 6–1012 (fols. 57–116) 118 (fols. 117–124; seventh cancelled; sixth, two strips, foliated 122 and 123) 12–1612 (fols. 125–184) 178 (fols. 185–200) 182 (fol. 201, wants second, stubs showing before Q17). The secundo folio of ‘tropologicus’ quoted on the back cover shows that the first quires were lost early on, and by 1516 when a list of electio books at Merton College (see History) refers to it by this secundo folio. The medieval foliation was added after this loss. Catchwords are given by all scribes horizontally at text size, under the written space at the inner edge. Most also chose to box them in a hairline cartouche (underlined on 116v). Vestiges only of catchword on 148v.

layoutDesc.layout: Ruled faintly in plummet and sometimes dry point for 36–44 long lines. Bounding rules are singles and pass to the edges. No visible prickings.

handDesc.handNote: The writing is in a number of German cursive hands at libraria level, datable broadly to the first decades of the fifteenth century. The main scribe of part I wrote a Hybrida and, for the first words of the text proper, a German Fractura. He goes to 110v, l. 26. A new hand, rather looser in a blacker ink, takes over mid-sentence at l. 27 and goes to the end of 120r. Abbreviations are much used in both and punctuation is minimal, a double virgule to mark sententiae. A further, contemporary German hand, well made and in a brown ink, supplied item 2 on blank leaves at the back of the quire.

There are two scribes for part II, the main scribe for this portion uses an upright, heavily shaded Cursiva with hairline finishing, the letters separated and consistent, going from 125r to the end of 190v (the close of the sixth sermon). Ink is black, going to dark brown.

A different scribe supplied the final sermon, 191r to the end. Like the first scribe of part I, this man also employed a German Fractura for the first words of the text. In both of these performances, the use of abbreviations and suspensions is limited. Punctuation is by punctus only for the first scribe, eschewed entirely by the second.

decoDesc.decoNote: Blank spaces were left for initials (guide letters provided), of five lines for the start of books and new texts and four for minor initials (two-line in the sermon section).
The only one to have been fulfilled is a five-line I on 125r, a simple outline initial in red ink.

Red stroking, underlining and the introduction of paraphs picks up suddenly on 23r, the start of c. 2 (although there is no change in the hand here), and halts at the foot of 25r. It would seem to be the esprit of a reader.

additions.p: The whole volume has been plentifully annotated—the commentary on Genesis particularly—in cursive hands. Many, if not most, of these belong to Henry of Abingdon (d. 1437), writing in various registers. They are largely navigational notes, supplying headwords in the margins or the names of biblical books referenced in the text; these latter Henry wrote larger and bolder. Others are brief notae (for example, ‘de logica’, ‘de scientia iuris’). One loosely made, sketchy manicula appears often in the Genesis commentary, sometimes in combination with a wavy line in the margin. Again, this appears to be Henry’s mark, for it is used in conjunction with notes in his hand on, for example, 73v and 74r (validity of the eucharist, comprehension of the Hebrew alphabet). A very different style of manicule is on 88v, done with some artistry, pointing to a statement on the natural pleasure music can give, making reference to Boethius; with the same man and similar concerns at 30r (celestial colours) and 52v (the nature of art). One man, who may once again have been Henry, entered a running heading on the recto sides, small and in pale ink (‘cam pm’ for ‘capitulum primum’, down to ‘ca 8’).

binding.p: A medieval tacketed binding with a wrapper which is a papal bull dated 18 February 1415 in favour of the book’s former owner, Henry of Abingdon (see above, fol. 1). The original creases remain from when the bull was kept folded (four across and two down, perhaps another hidden at the spine). It is sewn on upside down with the plica at the head, the lower edge is also turned in to fit the size of the text-block. The principal station for the long-stitch primary tacketing is at the centre of the spine, to exterior supports taken through a spine stiffener of thick tanned leather; primary tacketing is also found at head and tail. The edges of the wrapper at head and tail have been reinforced with overcast stitching. At the fore-edge of the back cover are the cross-stitch holes to show that a piece of parchment was once sewn on here to provide a fore-edge flap. This would have had ties fastening on to buttons on the spine: one of these leather buttons is still in situ at the foot of the spine stiffener; the hole for another is at the head. The volume was kept until recently within modern millboards covered in purple buckram with blank paper pastedowns and a lost textile tie at the centre of the fore-edge. These boards were formerly adhered to the volume by buckram inner joints, but have recently been detached and the joint strips removed for conservation reasons.

history.provenance: Labels and marks: There are many, now faded marks on the outside of the front cover (foliated 1). Two marks in brown ink and of the mid-fifteenth century relate to the volume’s presence at Merton College, Oxford. On the outer front cover is ‘Collegio de Merton in Oxonia’ and inside the cover on the upper turn-in is ‘Liber M. Henrici Abyndon’ | Custodis de Mertonhalle in Oxon’ | Et quem dedit eidem Collegio’. (For Henry of Abingdon, see History.) Beneath this is ‘secundo folio questiones 13’. These are all in the same hand, which may well have been Abingdon’s own. Also on the outer wrapper, at the head, is the titulus ‘Expositio super prologum Sacre scripture cum variis sentenciis’ (repeated beneath in a seventeenth-century hand, reading ‘variis sermonibus’). In the upper outer corner is the number ‘80’ in black ink, probably a Merton mark. Any James number has been lost with the first leaves. Below the centre line of the upper cover was written Lincoln’s early-modern pressmark, ‘E. 43. 3’. As in Lat. 110, this man continued by writing a title underneath: ‘Hieronymi sive incerti Auctoris opusculum’. The modern Bodleian shelf-mark is pencilled at the foot of the first page, 2r: ‘MS. Linc. Coll. (d) Lat. 62’; alongside it is the nineteenth-century mark ‘Linc. MS. 62 B 28’, repeated at the foot of fol. 10r, the first page of the next quire. On the spine are found the usual small, square labels: at the head, a printed number ‘28’; and at the foot, the Victorian blue-bordered label rotated through ninety degrees with ‘62’ in ink, and below that the pale-blue Bodleian label with the modern shelf-mark.

The manuscript was copied by German scribes perhaps a couple of decades after the Council of Constance, and it passed into the ownership of an Englishman, Henry of Abingdon (d. 1437), warden of Merton College, who inscribed his ex dono inside the cover on the upper turn-in (i.e. the plica of the bull): ‘Liber M. Henrici Abyndon’ | Custodis de Mertonhalle in Oxon’ | Et quem dedit eidem Collegio’. Henry of Abingdon was a figure of some reputation in the university of Oxford in the early fifteenth century. (His career was established by Emden, BRUO 7–8, and M. Harvey in an article in ODNB; see also A. N. E. D. Schofield, ‘The second English delegation to the Council of Basel’, JEH 17 (1966) 29–64.) His connections were with Merton College, where he held a fellowship by 1390 and was warden from 1421 until his death. There are indentures recording the distribution of books among the fellows from the warden’s collection during his time (see Thomson, Oxford, UO52), and as well as our manuscript, he also gave to Merton MSS 10 (Grosseteste’s Dicta and the Opus imperfectum in Matthaeum) and 154 (William of Milton’s Commentary on Ecclesiasticus). He was ordained priest in 1399 and admitted to the vicarage of Weston Zoyland in Somerset on 24 March 1403. Already by then a doctor of theology, in 1415 he received a papal indult to continue to enjoy the fruits of this benefice though absent for purposes of study: his copy of this document forms the wrapper of our manuscript (fols. 1, 202). He seems to have spent most of his career either at Oxford or, latterly, fulfilling his residentiary duties at Wells, where he was admitted to a prebendal stall in 1410 which he held until his death. Clearly esteemed at Oxford, he was chosen to be the university’s delegate to the Council of Constance in 1415. There, he defended the university's claim to precedence over Salamanca, and also (successfully) the priority of England over Spain. He also preached in 1417 a notable sermon against the clerical abuses of exemptions and simony (inc. ‘Sitis repleti fructu iustitie (Phil. 1:11) . . . Celestis agricola dominus Iesus Christus, veniens in mundum’); this sermon is found in two contemporary continental manuscripts (at ÖNB and Stuttgart; ed. C. W. F. Walch, Monimenta medii aevi, 6 pts in 2 vols (Göttingen 1757–61), 1/2. 183–205). He was granted leave to attend the Council of Basel in December of 1432; and in late 1434 he was appointed one of the proctors at Basel of Archbishop Chichele, and in July 1435 of the bishop of Bath and Wells. It is his presence at these two great councils that explains the appearance of this manuscript. At Constance he obtained the papal bull and at Basel the book itself, in tacketed quires. (The date of the scribes’ handwriting would be a better fit for the 1430s, affirming Basel.) Back in Oxford, he reused as a wrapper the papal bull which he no longer needed, since he was no longer absent in Oxford for study and had in any case surrendered Weston Zoyland.

The manuscript’s medieval history emerges from the recoverable inscriptions on the cover, now much rubbed and mostly only legible under ultraviolet light, for which, see Labels and marks. For a while, the manuscript remained in Henry of Abingdon’s possession. At one point he went in for a short-term loan with Elias Stokes in exchange for a book of sermons, as a faint, upside-down inscription on the front cover suggests: ‘Trad M. Henr’ Abyndone et / ?concedat ad usum M. / Helye Stokes / et ?neci pro sermonibus’ (as first read by Thomson, ‘Lincoln College MS lat. 62’, 259). Elias Stoke was a contemporary of Abingdon’s, rector of Exeter College from October 1391 until October 1393; he died between May and June 1436 (BRUO 1780).

His ex dono states that he then gave the book to Merton, where it entered the electio stock for circulation among the fellowship. On the back cover is the record of one election: ‘17us de sorte Nolo 2o fo. ?Questiones dei concepcionis 27us tropologicus’. The correction to the secundo folio reference shows that the manuscript had lost its front quires early on. (The name ‘Nolo’ is puzzling: Thomson (p. 260) suggests it may represent a name such as Noel or Nowell, but no such fellow is known.) It was reported by the same secundo folio (‘tropologice’) in 1516 in an inventory of theology books distributed in election (Thomson, Oxford, UO66. 388). Our manuscript was one of quite a number which came loose from Merton in the course of the seventeenth century, many to be found now in the Bodleian. The route this one took to Lincoln is not known, but it came to the College after the rebinding campaign of the 1620s and before 1697, when it was reported at Lincoln for the Bernard catalogue (no. 1401).
